screens.title: Structured Streaming (Batch Perspective)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll treat Structured Streaming as an extension of the batch world you already know. Structured Streaming lets you write the same DataFrame and Dataset code you use for batch jobs and run it continuously, processing newly arriving data in small, regular micro-batches. You will learn how to use Databricks Auto Loader to detect new files in an ADLS Gen2 landing zone, how to add processing timestamps and transform streams as if they were static tables, and how to write results to Delta Lake with durable checkpointing. This approach reduces latency compared with once-a-day batch jobs and fits common cloud ingestion patterns where files arrive periodically. I'll show a practical micro-batch ingestion pattern, discuss output modes like append and complete, and explain why checkpointLocation on durable storage is essential to avoid data loss and duplicates. By the end you'll understand when to convert a batch job into a micro-batched stream and how to set up safe, repeatable streaming writes to Delta. Think about the last scenario where fresh data would speed decisions — that is where micro-batch streaming helps most.

screens.title: What is Structured Streaming?
screens.narratorSegment: Structured Streaming is Spark's stream-processing A P I that treats a stream as an unbounded table and executes your S Q L or DataFrame operations incrementally. In practical terms, that means you write transformations, filters, and aggregations the same way you would for a static dataset, and Spark runs micro-batches to apply those operations as new data arrives. This lowers the learning curve: familiar batch code becomes streaming code with spark. readStream and writeStream. A core benefit is fault tolerance: the engine records progress and state to checkpoint locations so that, on failure, the stream resumes without reprocessing already committed data. A common use case from a batch perspective is processing newly landed files in a directory — rather than running a large nightly job, you run small, frequent micro-batches to keep tables up to date. One misconception is that streaming always means complex event processing; in many cloud ingestion patterns, streaming is simply a scheduled, automated way to process files as they appear. To test your understanding, ask whether your logic relies on previously seen data — if it does, you must consider state, checkpointing, and an appropriate output mode. What part of your current batch pipeline would benefit most from lower latency?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Structured Streaming provides an incremental execution model so DataFrame transformations can run continuously with fault tolerance and familiar semantics.

content.html:
Core Concept
Structured Streaming
Treat a stream as an unbounded table and run incremental DataFrame operations as micro-batches.
Why it matters
  • Reuses batch code, reducing mistakes when converting jobs.
  • Supports exactly-once semantics with checkpointing on durable storage.
  • Enables fresher data and faster insights than daily batch runs.
Analogy
Think of a timer that runs the same batch job every minute over only new files.
Common misconception
Streaming always requires complex event processing — not true for file-based micro-batches.
Streaming as a Batch Extension
Use the same DataFrame API but with spark.readStream and writeStream and let Spark manage incremental runs.
Quick example
# Create a streaming DataFrame from files
streaming_df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") \
  .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv") \
  .schema(sales_schema) \
  .load(input_path)

# Apply batch-like transformations
processed = streaming_df.withColumn("IngestionTime", current_timestamp())
Key Takeaway

You can treat incoming files as an unbounded table and run familiar batch transforms incrementally with durable state.

screens.title: Micro-batch processing pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Micro-batch processing breaks a continuous stream into repeated small jobs that process only the newly arrived data. The typical flow starts with a landing zone on ADLS Gen2 where external systems drop files. Databricks Auto Loader or a file-based readStream detects these new files without listing the entire directory, then Spark creates a micro-batch that reads just the new records. Within the micro-batch you run the same transformations you would in a batch job: parsing, enrichment, adding a processing timestamp, and optional aggregations. The stream writer writes results to a sink — often a Delta table or path — and Spark records progress and state in the checkpointLocation so the next micro-batch resumes safely. Triggers control how often Spark checks for new data; for example processingTime="1 minute" processes every minute. A common pitfall is using transient storage for the checkpointLocation; if a job fails and checkpoint metadata is lost, the engine may reprocess or skip data. Another nuance is choosing the right outputMode: append is efficient for new rows, but aggregations often need complete or update modes. When designing micro-batches, consider file arrival rate, processing time, and checkpoint durability so your pipeline remains both fresh and correct.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Files arrive → Auto Loader detects → micro-batch reads new data → transforms run → results written to sink → checkpoint updated for fault tolerance.

content.html:
Process Flow
Micro-batch steps
  1. Files are dropped into the landing directory on ADLS Gen2.
  2. Auto Loader discovers new files incrementally and hands paths to Spark.
  3. Spark runs a micro-batch: readStream, transformations, aggregations.
  4. Results are written to Delta or another sink; checkpoint is updated.
Design considerations
  • Choose checkpointLocation on durable storage like ADLS Gen2.
  • Set trigger interval based on file arrival rate and processing time.
  • Pick an outputMode compatible with your aggregation logic.
Visual flow (cards)
Landing Zone
ADLS Gen2
Auto Loader
cloudFiles
Delta Sink
Append or Complete
Example
New CSV files dropped every few minutes are processed with processingTime 1 minute to update daily aggregates.
Common mistake
Using append with a groupBy aggregation without a watermark can produce incorrect results or require complete mode.
Key Takeaway

Micro-batch pipelines let you process files incrementally; planning triggers, output modes, and checkpointing is essential for correctness and durability.

screens.title: Reading files with Auto Loader
screens.narratorSegment: Auto Loader, exposed via cloudFiles in Databricks, is the recommended way to ingest files from a cloud directory efficiently. It avoids expensive full-directory listings by using cloud notifications or incremental file listing, which scales to large data lakes. In code, you call spark. readStream. format with cloudFiles, set cloudFiles. format to the file type such as csv, and provide a schema rather than inferring it in production. You also set a schemaLocation under your checkpoint directory so Auto Loader can persist inferred schema details and evolutions. A practical example is reading sales CSVs from a mounted ADLS Gen2 input path and wiring the options to cloudFiles. schemaLocation and header true. One misconception is that Auto Loader processes file contents differently — it simply optimizes discovery and hands files to Spark for normal streaming reads. For safety, do not rely on schema inference in production; explicit schema avoids subtle evolution surprises. In the lab, you'll simulate arrival by writing files into the input path and observing how Auto Loader picks up new batches. Reading files with Auto Loader means auto loader reduces file discovery cost and scales to large directories while preserving standard structured streaming semantics.. In practical terms, using spark.readstream.format("cloudfiles") for efficient file discovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Auto Loader usage pattern
streaming_df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") \
  .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv") \
  .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", f"{checkpoint_location}/schema") \
  .option("header", "true") \
  .schema(sales_schema) \
  .load(input_path)

# Add processing time column
processed = streaming_df.withColumn("ProcessingTimestamp", current_timestamp())
Note: use an explicit schema for production and set cloudFiles.schemaLocation to a durable subdirectory under your checkpointLocation.
Practical example
If your landing zone receives dozens of files per minute, Auto Loader avoids repeated expensive directory listings and supports schema evolution when configured with a schema location.
Example scenario
Sensor CSV files are dropped periodically; Auto Loader fetches new files and Spark runs a micro-batch to append them into a raw Delta table.
Misconception
Auto Loader changes how data is parsed — false. Parsing is done by Spark; Auto Loader optimizes discovery and handing off files.
Key Takeaway

Prefer cloudFiles (Auto Loader) for scalable file discovery and set an explicit schema with a schemaLocation under a durable checkpoint path.

screens.title: Schema and streaming transformations
screens.narratorSegment: A robust streaming pipeline starts with an explicit schema. By defining a StructType up front you avoid unpredictable schema inference during runtime and ensure consistent column types for aggregations. For example, define OrderID, OrderDate as TimestampType, Quantity as Integer, and TotalAmount as Double. After reading, add an ingestion timestamp using current_timestamp and derive fields such as OrderDay by casting an order date to date. These transformations are identical to batch operations, but they run inside each micro-batch. One important difference is stateful operations: when you perform groupBy with aggregations across batches, Spark maintains aggregation state that is checkpointed. For windowed aggregations add watermarks to bound state size. A common mistake is relying on implicit casts or late schema changes; if a new column appears with a different type it can break the stream. The safe pattern is explicit schema, minimal implicit casting, and validating results after a short run. This prepares you to write aggregated or enriched results reliably into Delta. Schema and streaming transformations means use explicit schema and deterministic transformations; for stateful aggregation add watermarks and checkpoint state durably.. In practical terms, define schemas and apply safe transformations to streaming dataframes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe transforms
keyIdea.text: Use explicit schema and deterministic transformations; for stateful aggregation add watermarks and checkpoint state durably.

content.html:
Definition
Explicit schema example
sales_schema = StructType([
  StructField("OrderID", StringType(), True),
  StructField("CustomerID", StringType(), True),
  StructField("OrderDate", TimestampType(), True),
  StructField("ProductCategory", StringType(), True),
  StructField("Quantity", IntegerType(), True),
  StructField("TotalAmount", DoubleType(), True)
])
Define types explicitly to prevent runtime parsing errors and to keep aggregation state consistent across micro-batches.
Transformations
Use withColumn for derived fields, cast to date for day-level aggregation, and add ingestion timestamps for traceability.
processed_streaming_df = streaming_df \
  .withColumn("ProcessingTimestamp", current_timestamp()) \
  .withColumn("OrderDay", col("OrderDate").cast("date"))
Example
Cast OrderDate to date to compute daily totals using groupBy on OrderDay and ProductCategory.
Pitfall
Allowing schema inference in production can lead to type mismatches when sources evolve.
Pro Tip

Validate a short run of the stream and inspect the schema files under schemaLocation before going to production.

screens.title: Output modes: append, complete, update
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the correct outputMode is crucial for correctness and performance. Append mode writes only new rows produced in the current micro-batch. It's efficient for file sinks and simple streaming inserts where existing rows are not changed. Complete mode writes the entire updated result table every trigger — this is often necessary for aggregations that recompute the full state, for example daily totals by category. Complete mode can be heavy for large state sizes and requires a sink that can handle full rewrites. Update mode writes only rows that have changed since the last trigger and can be a middle ground but has conditions and limits depending on the sink. A common error is mixing append with aggregations that update previous keys; in that case append will not reflect corrected totals. For aggregations, consider using watermarks to bound state and choose complete when you need the full aggregated snapshot, mindful of sink capabilities. Always match your outputMode with both the type of computation and the sink's semantics to avoid incorrect results or write errors. Output modes: append, complete, update means use append for new rows, complete for full aggregation snapshots, and update when only changed rows should be written — ensure sink compatibility.. In practical terms, choose the right mode for file sinks and aggregations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Output mode selection
keyIdea.text: Use append for new rows, complete for full aggregation snapshots, and update when only changed rows should be written — ensure sink compatibility.

content.html:
Comparison
Append
Writes only newly-produced rows. Good for file sinks where each micro-batch adds new records.
Best when you are not updating previous keys.
Complete
Writes the entire result table every trigger. Useful for aggregated snapshots but heavier on sink.
Use for groupBy aggregations that update prior keys.
Update
Writes only rows that changed since the last trigger. Often limited by sink semantics and requirements.
Choose when supported and when you need incremental updates of stateful results.
Concrete example
If you compute daily totals by product category and need the full snapshot each minute for downstream dashboards, complete mode gives a full view. If you only append raw event rows to a Delta raw table, append mode is best.
Misconception
Append is always cheaper — append can be wrong when prior rows must change as new data arrives.
Key Takeaway

Match outputMode to the computation and sink. Aggregations often need complete or update; simple inserts can use append.

screens.title: Writing to Delta Lake and sinks
screens.narratorSegment: Writing streaming results into Delta Lake provides ACID semantics and works well with Structured Streaming. You can write to a managed table in the Hive Metastore using toTable, or write to a path with start(output_path) to create an unmanaged Delta table. For streams that append raw rows, choose append mode. For aggregation results that update state, choose complete or update depending on sink support. Always set checkpointLocation to a durable ADLS Gen2 path so offsets, schemas, and state are persisted. One practical pattern is to write raw ingested records to a raw Delta table in append mode, and write aggregated summaries to a curated Delta table using complete mode at a longer trigger interval. A typical write call includes. format("delta"),. option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_location), and a trigger. A frequent misconception is that Delta automatically isolates you from all streaming concerns — Delta helps with durability and schema enforcement, but it does not replace good choices about outputMode, triggers, and checkpointing. Design sinks with the table size and rewrite cost in mind. Writing to Delta Lake and sinks means use format 'delta', choose managed vs unmanaged table appropriately, and always configure checkpointlocation for durable state and safe restarts.. In practical terms, durable writes and managed vs unmanaged tables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Delta writes
keyIdea.text: Use format 'delta', choose managed vs unmanaged table appropriately, and always configure checkpointLocation for durable state and safe restarts.

content.html:
Architecture
Delta write pattern
query = daily_summary_df.writeStream \
  .format("delta") \
  .outputMode("complete") \
  .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_location) \
  .trigger(processingTime="1 minute") \
  .toTable("daily_sales_summary")

# Alternatively, for an unmanaged table or path:
# .start(output_delta_path)
Choose .toTable for managed tables that appear in the metastore; use .start(path) to manage files directly.
Key Takeaway

Delta offers durable, transactional writes for streams, but you must choose output mode and checkpointing to keep results correct and efficient.

Managed vs Unmanaged
Managed tables live in the metastore and are convenient for queries; unmanaged tables let you control physical layout and paths.
Example pattern

screens.title: Checkpointing for fault tolerance
screens.narratorSegment: Checkpointing is the mechanism Structured Streaming uses to remember what it has processed and to store aggregation state. The checkpointLocation is a directory on durable storage that contains offset progress, schema snapshots when using Auto Loader, and any state for aggregations. If a streaming query fails, Spark uses the checkpoint to resume from the last committed micro-batch and avoids reprocessing data that was already handled. This is why placing the checkpointLocation on transient storage is a critical mistake — if the checkpoint directory is lost, the stream may reprocess or skip data when restarted. Checkpoint directories should be shared among driver restarts but isolated per streaming query. In practice, create a stable path under your ADLS Gen2 mount and point checkpointLocation there. For stateful aggregations, the checkpoint will also store interim aggregation state, which is why adding watermarks is important to prevent unbounded state growth. Always verify the checkpoint directory after a test run to ensure schema and progress files appear as expected. Checkpointing for fault tolerance means checkpoint stores progress, schema metadata, and aggregation state so streams can restart exactly once and avoid duplicates or data loss.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Triggers and processing intervals
screens.narratorSegment: Triggers determine when Spark checks for new data and starts a micro-batch. The most common trigger is processingTime, for example processingTime="1 minute", which schedules a micro-batch roughly every minute. Setting the interval too short can cause overlapping batches if processing time exceeds the trigger; too long increases latency. Another option is once mode which runs a single micro-batch and exits — useful for scheduled micro-batch runs that act like batch jobs. Choosing triggers should consider file arrival patterns and average micro-batch duration. If files arrive in bursts, a slightly longer trigger with larger batches may be more efficient. If low latency is required, use shorter triggers but ensure the cluster can complete work within the interval. A misconception is that a shorter trigger always improves latency — if processing cannot complete in time, it increases backlog and instability. Tune triggers based on observed processing time and throughput. Trigger options

Start with a conservative interval and monitor; adjust as you observe average batch durations and throughput.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll treat Structured Streaming as an extension of the batch world you already know. Structured Streaming lets you write the same DataFrame and Dataset code you use for batch jobs and run it continuously, processing newly arriving data in small, regular micro-batches. You will learn how to use Databricks Auto Loader to detect new files in an ADLS Gen2 landing zone, how to add processing timestamps and transform streams as if they were static tables, and how to write results to Delta Lake with durable checkpointing. This approach reduces latency compared with once-a-day batch jobs and fits common cloud ingestion patterns where files arrive periodically. I'll show a practical micro-batch ingestion pattern, discuss output modes like append and complete, and explain why checkpointLocation on durable storage is essential to avoid data loss and duplicates. By the end you'll understand when to convert a batch job into a micro-batched stream and how to set up safe, repeatable streaming writes to Delta. Think about the last scenario where fresh data would speed decisions — that is where micro-batch streaming helps most.

These learning objectives map directly to practical skills you'll use in Databricks. First, you will understand Structured Streaming as a micro-batch engine and be able to explain how it relates to batch processing and why it reduces data latency. Second, you'll be able to distinguish batch and streaming sources and sinks inside Structured Streaming, recognizing when a file directory can be treated as a streaming input. Third, you'll implement a streaming job that reads files from ADLS Gen2 using Auto Loader or standard readStream formats, applying schema and transformations safely. Finally, you'll configure writes to Delta Lake and set up checkpointing so your job restarts without reprocessing data. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can prove competency by running a short ingestion pipeline and validating results in a Delta table. These are practical, hands-on outcomes designed for the Databricks environment used in the lab activity, and they focus on reliability, correctness, and low-latency data delivery.

Beyond conceptual understanding, this chapter targets hands-on outcomes. You should be able to define input and output paths in ADLS Gen2, create or reference a durable checkpoint directory, and construct a streaming DataFrame with spark. readStream using either Auto Loader or a file format like CSV. You'll add a processing timestamp column and simple aggregates, then write the results into a Delta table or path with an appropriate outputMode. In the lab you'll simulate file arrival, run the stream for a short period, and validate that both the first and later files appear in the Delta table. Finally, you'll inspect the streaming query in the Databricks UI to verify batch durations and check that the checkpoint folder contains schema and progress metadata. Each of these steps proves that you can convert batch ingestion into a reliable micro-batch pipeline with durable state and repeatable results.

Structured Streaming is Spark's stream-processing A P I that treats a stream as an unbounded table and executes your S Q L or DataFrame operations incrementally. In practical terms, that means you write transformations, filters, and aggregations the same way you would for a static dataset, and Spark runs micro-batches to apply those operations as new data arrives. This lowers the learning curve: familiar batch code becomes streaming code with spark. readStream and writeStream. A core benefit is fault tolerance: the engine records progress and state to checkpoint locations so that, on failure, the stream resumes without reprocessing already committed data. A common use case from a batch perspective is processing newly landed files in a directory — rather than running a large nightly job, you run small, frequent micro-batches to keep tables up to date. One misconception is that streaming always means complex event processing; in many cloud ingestion patterns, streaming is simply a scheduled, automated way to process files as they appear. To test your understanding, ask whether your logic relies on previously seen data — if it does, you must consider state, checkpointing, and an appropriate output mode. What part of your current batch pipeline would benefit most from lower latency?

Micro-batch processing breaks a continuous stream into repeated small jobs that process only the newly arrived data. The typical flow starts with a landing zone on ADLS Gen2 where external systems drop files. Databricks Auto Loader or a file-based readStream detects these new files without listing the entire directory, then Spark creates a micro-batch that reads just the new records. Within the micro-batch you run the same transformations you would in a batch job: parsing, enrichment, adding a processing timestamp, and optional aggregations. The stream writer writes results to a sink — often a Delta table or path — and Spark records progress and state in the checkpointLocation so the next micro-batch resumes safely. Triggers control how often Spark checks for new data; for example processingTime="1 minute" processes every minute. A common pitfall is using transient storage for the checkpointLocation; if a job fails and checkpoint metadata is lost, the engine may reprocess or skip data. Another nuance is choosing the right outputMode: append is efficient for new rows, but aggregations often need complete or update modes. When designing micro-batches, consider file arrival rate, processing time, and checkpoint durability so your pipeline remains both fresh and correct.

Auto Loader, exposed via cloudFiles in Databricks, is the recommended way to ingest files from a cloud directory efficiently. It avoids expensive full-directory listings by using cloud notifications or incremental file listing, which scales to large data lakes. In code, you call spark. readStream. format with cloudFiles, set cloudFiles. format to the file type such as csv, and provide a schema rather than inferring it in production. You also set a schemaLocation under your checkpoint directory so Auto Loader can persist inferred schema details and evolutions. A practical example is reading sales CSVs from a mounted ADLS Gen2 input path and wiring the options to cloudFiles. schemaLocation and header true. One misconception is that Auto Loader processes file contents differently — it simply optimizes discovery and hands files to Spark for normal streaming reads. For safety, do not rely on schema inference in production; explicit schema avoids subtle evolution surprises. In the lab, you'll simulate arrival by writing files into the input path and observing how Auto Loader picks up new batches. Reading files with Auto Loader means auto loader reduces file discovery cost and scales to large directories while preserving standard structured streaming semantics.. In practical terms, using spark.readstream.format("cloudfiles") for efficient file discovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A robust streaming pipeline starts with an explicit schema. By defining a StructType up front you avoid unpredictable schema inference during runtime and ensure consistent column types for aggregations. For example, define OrderID, OrderDate as TimestampType, Quantity as Integer, and TotalAmount as Double. After reading, add an ingestion timestamp using current_timestamp and derive fields such as OrderDay by casting an order date to date. These transformations are identical to batch operations, but they run inside each micro-batch. One important difference is stateful operations: when you perform groupBy with aggregations across batches, Spark maintains aggregation state that is checkpointed. For windowed aggregations add watermarks to bound state size. A common mistake is relying on implicit casts or late schema changes; if a new column appears with a different type it can break the stream. Selecting the correct outputMode is crucial for correctness and performance. Append mode writes only new rows produced in the current micro-batch. It's efficient for file sinks and simple streaming inserts where existing rows are not changed. Complete mode writes the entire updated result table every trigger — this is often necessary for aggregations that recompute the full state, for example daily totals by category. Complete mode can be heavy for large state sizes and requires a sink that can handle full rewrites. Update mode writes only rows that have changed since the last trigger and can be a middle ground but has conditions and limits depending on the sink. A common error is mixing append with aggregations that update previous keys; in that case append will not reflect corrected totals.
